questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) in network security?
questions.option_a: To provide a separate network segment for public-facing services while protecting the internal network from direct exposure.
questions.option_b: To encrypt all communication between internal and external networks.
questions.option_c: To allow unrestricted communication between the Internet and internal servers.
questions.option_d: To replace the need for firewalls at the network perimeter.
questions.explanation: A DMZ is a buffer network segment that hosts externally accessible services without directly exposing the trusted internal network.

questions.question: A company hosts a public web server inside its DMZ. An attacker successfully compromises the server. What is the main security benefit provided by the DMZ?
questions.option_a: The compromised server automatically loses its Internet connectivity.
questions.option_b: The attacker cannot execute any additional commands on the compromised server.
questions.option_c: The attacker does not automatically obtain a direct path into the internal network.
questions.option_d: The firewall automatically restores the compromised server to its original state.
questions.explanation: A DMZ contains the potential damage by separating public-facing systems from the internal network. It does not prevent the initial compromise.

questions.question: Which of the following services would most appropriately be hosted in a DMZ?
questions.option_a: An internal employee payroll database accessible only to finance staff.
questions.option_b: A public-facing web server that must accept connections from Internet users.
questions.option_c: An internal domain controller responsible for employee authentication.
questions.option_d: A private workstation used by the network administrator.
questions.explanation: Public-facing services such as web, email, and DNS servers are appropriate DMZ candidates because they need external accessibility.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between a DMZ and the internal network?
questions.option_a: The DMZ is a trusted extension of the internal network with unrestricted access.
questions.option_b: The DMZ eliminates the need to control traffic entering the internal network.
questions.option_c: The DMZ and internal network must always share the same subnet.
questions.option_d: The DMZ acts as a buffer between the untrusted external network and the trusted internal network.
questions.explanation: The DMZ separates externally exposed services from internal resources, reducing the impact of a compromised public-facing system.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes the security objective of a DMZ?
questions.option_a: Preventing every possible attack against public-facing servers.
questions.option_b: Allowing public-facing servers to access all internal resources.
questions.option_c: Containing potential damage by restricting access from compromised DMZ systems to the internal network.
questions.option_d: Replacing internal network segmentation with a single perimeter firewall.
questions.explanation: A DMZ is designed to limit the consequences of compromise through network separation and restricted traffic paths.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a Zone-Based Firewall (ZBF)?
questions.option_a: To introduce a completely new packet inspection technology.
questions.option_b: To organise firewall policies around logical network zones rather than individual interface pairs.
questions.option_c: To eliminate the requirement for access control policies.
questions.option_d: To assign dynamic IP addresses to devices in different network segments.
questions.explanation: ZBF is a configuration model that organises security policies around logical zones such as INSIDE, OUTSIDE, and DMZ.

questions.question: In a typical Zone-Based Firewall configuration, what happens to traffic moving between two different zones when no explicit zone-pair policy permits it?
questions.option_a: It is denied by default.
questions.option_b: It is automatically permitted if the destination is reachable.
questions.option_c: It is forwarded only if both zones use the same subnet.
questions.option_d: It is permitted when the source zone is INSIDE.
questions.explanation: Traffic between different zones is denied by default unless an explicit zone-pair policy allows it.

questions.question: Which statement describes the default behaviour of traffic within the same Zone-Based Firewall zone according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: All traffic is denied regardless of its destination.
questions.option_b: Traffic must pass through an OUTSIDE-to-INSIDE policy.
questions.option_c: Traffic is permitted only when a Named ACL is configured.
questions.option_d: Traffic within the same zone is typically allowed by default.
questions.explanation: The lecture states that traffic within the same zone is typically allowed by default, unlike traffic between different zones.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid example of a Zone-Based Firewall configuration?
questions.option_a: Creating separate logical zones named INSIDE, OUTSIDE, and DMZ and assigning interfaces to them.
questions.option_b: Assigning every network interface a separate public IP address without defining policies.
questions.option_c: Replacing all firewall inspection mechanisms with subnet masks.
questions.option_d: Allowing communication between all zones without defining zone-pair policies.
questions.explanation: ZBF groups interfaces into logical zones and applies policies between those zones.

questions.question: Could a Packet Filtering firewall be configured using the Zone-Based Firewall model?
questions.option_a: No, because ZBF requires a dedicated application-layer firewall.
questions.option_b: No, because packet filtering cannot operate between different network zones.
questions.option_c: Yes, because ZBF organises policies and does not define a new inspection technology.
questions.option_d: Yes, but only when all interfaces belong to the same zone.
questions.explanation: ZBF is a configuration model rather than an inspection technology. Any of the seven firewall types discussed in the earlier lecture can operate underneath it.

questions.question: Which firewall placement architecture uses a single firewall positioned after the border router?
questions.option_a: Dual firewall with the router between both firewalls.
questions.option_b: Single firewall behind the border router.
questions.option_c: Single firewall in front of the border router.
questions.option_d: Dual firewall with the router before both firewalls.
questions.explanation: In this architecture, traffic passes from the Internet through the border router before reaching the single firewall.

questions.question: Which is a major advantage of placing a single firewall in front of the border router?
questions.option_a: It eliminates the possibility of firewall failure.
questions.option_b: It removes the need for routing protocols.
questions.option_c: It automatically provides two independent security boundaries.
questions.option_d: It filters Internet traffic before it reaches the router, protecting the router itself.
questions.explanation: The firewall inspects and filters traffic before it reaches the border router, providing direct protection to the router.

questions.question: Which placement architecture provides defence in depth using two firewalls with the router positioned before both firewalls?
questions.option_a: Dual firewall, router before both.
questions.option_b: Single firewall behind the border router.
questions.option_c: Single firewall in front of the border router.
questions.option_d: Dual firewall, router between the two firewalls.
questions.explanation: This screened-subnet architecture uses two separate firewalls, with the router positioned before both security devices.

questions.question: Which architecture places the router between two firewalls?
questions.option_a: Single firewall behind the border router.
questions.option_b: Dual firewall, router before both.
questions.option_c: Dual firewall, router between the two.
questions.option_d: Single firewall in front of the border router.
questions.explanation: In this design, traffic encounters Firewall 1, then the router, and subsequently Firewall 2.

questions.question: What is a major disadvantage of using a single firewall behind the border router?
questions.option_a: It requires two separate firewall devices.
questions.option_b: The firewall cannot filter traffic based on network policies.
questions.option_c: The router must always be positioned between two firewalls.
questions.option_d: The firewall becomes a single point of failure for the network.
questions.explanation: If the only firewall fails, the network loses its primary firewall security boundary.

questions.question: Which is a potential weakness of placing a single firewall in front of the border router?
questions.option_a: The firewall cannot inspect inbound Internet traffic.
questions.option_b: Router management and routing-protocol traffic must also pass through firewall policy, increasing complexity.
questions.option_c: It requires three separate firewall devices.
questions.option_d: The router is completely isolated from the Internet and cannot perform routing.
questions.explanation: The router's own management and routing-protocol traffic must pass through the firewall, adding policy complexity.

questions.question: Which is a key advantage of the dual-firewall screened-subnet architecture?
questions.option_a: It eliminates all configuration and management overhead.
questions.option_b: It allows the DMZ to communicate freely with the internal network.
questions.option_c: An attacker must compromise two separate firewalls to reach the internal network through the intended path.
questions.option_d: It requires only one security device to protect the entire network.
questions.explanation: The architecture provides defence in depth through two separate firewall boundaries and an isolated DMZ.

questions.question: Which statement describes a disadvantage of the dual-firewall architecture with the router between both firewalls?
questions.option_a: The router may be exposed if Firewall 1 is bypassed because there is no second firewall immediately in front of it.
questions.option_b: It does not provide a second firewall for the internal network.
questions.option_c: It cannot separate the DMZ from the Internet.
questions.option_d: It requires all internal traffic to bypass both firewalls.
questions.explanation: Firewall 1 is the first security boundary. If it is bypassed, the router is exposed before traffic reaches Firewall 2.

questions.question: How are ACL statements evaluated when a packet is processed?
questions.option_a: From bottom to top until every statement has been checked.
questions.option_b: Randomly based on the packet protocol.
questions.option_c: In numerical order, regardless of their configured sequence.
questions.option_d: From top to bottom, stopping at the first matching statement.
questions.explanation: ACLs are ordered lists. The first matching permit or deny statement determines the packet's treatment.

questions.question: What happens when a packet does not match any explicitly configured statement in an ACL?
questions.option_a: The packet is permitted if its destination is reachable.
questions.option_b: The packet is denied by the implicit deny rule.
questions.option_c: The router forwards the packet to another ACL automatically.
questions.option_d: The packet is permitted when the ACL contains at least one permit statement.
questions.explanation: Every ACL ends with an invisible implicit deny. Packets that match no explicit statement are dropped.

questions.question: Which fields can a Standard ACL use to filter traffic?
questions.option_a: Source IP address only.
questions.option_b: Source and destination IP addresses.
questions.option_c: Source IP address, destination IP address, protocol, and port.
questions.option_d: Destination IP address and destination port only.
questions.explanation: Standard ACLs evaluate only the source IP address and cannot distinguish destinations, protocols, or ports.

questions.question: Which information can an Extended ACL examine when filtering packets?
questions.option_a: Source IP address only.
questions.option_b: Destination IP address only.
questions.option_c: Source and destination IP addresses, protocol, and source and destination ports.
questions.option_d: MAC addresses and physical switch port numbers only.
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs provide more precise matching by supporting source and destination addresses, protocols, and TCP/UDP ports.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a Named ACL and a numbered ACL?
questions.option_a: A Named ACL can filter application-layer traffic while numbered ACLs cannot.
questions.option_b: A Named ACL automatically permits established TCP connections.
questions.option_c: A Named ACL supports destination filtering while numbered ACLs only support source filtering.
questions.option_d: A Named ACL uses a descriptive identifier instead of a number and is easier to maintain.
questions.explanation: Named ACLs are functionally Standard or Extended ACLs. Their main advantage is readability and easier maintenance.

questions.question: Which number range identifies a Standard ACL?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies 1–99 and 1300–1999 as the numbered Standard ACL ranges.

questions.question: Which number range identifies an Extended ACL?
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs use the numbered ranges 100–199 and 2000–2699.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a wildcard mask in an ACL?
questions.option_a: To encrypt the source IP address.
questions.option_b: To specify which destination port should be blocked.
questions.option_c: To define the protocol used by a packet.
questions.option_d: To identify which IP address bits must match exactly and which bits can vary.
questions.explanation: A wildcard mask is the inverse of a subnet mask. A 0 requires an exact bit match, while a 1 allows that bit to vary.

questions.question: What does the host keyword represent in Standard or Extended ACL syntax?
questions.option_a: Any IP address within a network.
questions.option_b: A wildcard mask of 255.255.255.255.
questions.option_c: A single exact IP address using a wildcard mask of 0.0.0.0.
questions.option_d: A destination address with an automatically assigned subnet mask.
questions.explanation: The host keyword is shorthand for matching one exact IP address, equivalent to a wildcard mask of 0.0.0.0.

questions.question: Which placement rule is recommended for Standard ACLs?
questions.option_a: As close to the source as possible.
questions.option_b: As close to the destination as possible.
questions.option_c: Only on the Internet-facing border router.
questions.option_d: Only between two firewalls.
questions.explanation: Standard ACLs match only source IP addresses. Placing them near the destination reduces the risk of blocking traffic to unintended destinations.

questions.question: Which placement rule is recommended for Extended ACLs?
questions.option_a: As close to the source as possible.
questions.option_b: As close to the destination as possible.
questions.option_c: Only on the destination server.
questions.option_d: Only on interfaces connecting the DMZ to the Internet.
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs can precisely match source, destination, protocol, and ports, so unwanted traffic can be stopped close to its source.

questions.question: Which operator would be used in an Extended ACL to match TCP traffic destined for port 23?
questions.option_a: host
questions.option_b: established
questions.option_c: range
questions.option_d: eq
questions.explanation: The eq operator matches a specified port number or service name. For Telnet, the destination port is 23.

questions.question: What does the established keyword check in an Extended ACL?
questions.option_a: Whether a TCP packet contains a SYN flag.
questions.option_b: Whether a TCP packet has an ACK or RST flag set.
questions.option_c: Whether a UDP session has already completed a handshake.
questions.option_d: Whether the source and destination belong to the same subnet.
questions.explanation: The established keyword is TCP-specific and matches packets with ACK or RST set. A fresh SYN without ACK does not match.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a sequence number in a Named ACL?
questions.option_a: To identify the destination port of a packet.
questions.option_b: To determine which protocol is inspected first.
questions.option_c: To specify the exact position of an ACL statement and allow insertion or management of individual entries.
questions.option_d: To assign a unique IP address to every ACL entry.
questions.explanation: Sequence numbers allow administrators to insert or remove individual entries at specific positions without rebuilding the entire Named ACL.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid advantage of using a Named ACL?
questions.option_a: It automatically has a higher priority than numbered ACLs.
questions.option_b: It eliminates the implicit deny rule.
questions.option_c: It supports matching additional protocols unavailable to numbered ACLs.
questions.option_d: It allows administrators to use descriptive names and manage individual entries more easily.
questions.explanation: Named ACLs improve readability and maintainability. Their matching capabilities remain identical to their underlying Standard or Extended type.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the effect of applying an ACL to an interface?
questions.option_a: An ACL can be applied to an interface in an inbound or outbound direction, affecting which packets are evaluated.
questions.option_b: An ACL always filters traffic in both directions automatically.
questions.option_c: An ACL can only be applied to an interface in the outbound direction.
questions.option_d: An ACL application direction does not affect packet processing.
questions.explanation: ACLs are applied per interface and per direction. Inbound and outbound application can produce different filtering behaviour.

questions.question: A network administrator wants to block Telnet traffic from 192.168.10.0/24 to the specific server 192.168.20.5 while permitting all other traffic. Which ACL type is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: Standard ACL.
questions.option_b: Extended ACL.
questions.option_c: Standard Named ACL only.
questions.option_d: A Standard ACL with a destination port condition.
questions.explanation: The policy requires matching source subnet, destination host, TCP protocol, and destination port 23. Only an Extended ACL supports all these conditions.

questions.question: A router administrator needs to allow only the subnet 192.168.50.0/28 through an interface while denying all other source addresses. Which ACL type is sufficient?
questions.option_a: Extended ACL with TCP port matching.
questions.option_b: Extended ACL with destination host matching.
questions.option_c: Standard ACL matching the source subnet.
questions.option_d: Named ACL that permits all IP traffic.
questions.explanation: The policy depends only on the source address, so a Standard ACL is sufficient. The /28 wildcard mask is 0.0.0.15.

questions.question: A network administrator configures the following ACL: access-list 10 permit 192.168.100.0 0.0.0.31. What range of source addresses does this statement match?
questions.explanation: The wildcard mask 0.0.0.31 allows the final five bits to vary, matching the address block 192.168.100.0/27.

questions.question: A network administrator configures the following ACL: access-list 101 deny tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.20.5 eq 23. What traffic is denied?
questions.option_a: All TCP traffic from 192.168.20.5 to the 192.168.10.0/24 subnet.
questions.option_b: All UDP traffic from 192.168.10.0/24 to 192.168.20.5.
questions.option_c: All IP traffic between the two networks.
questions.option_d: TCP traffic from 192.168.10.0/24 to 192.168.20.5 with destination port 23.
questions.explanation: The ACL matches TCP traffic from the specified source subnet to the exact destination host, with destination port 23.

questions.question: A network administrator creates an Extended ACL containing only access-list 101 deny tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.20.5 eq 23. What happens to other traffic processed by this ACL?
questions.option_a: It is automatically permitted because the deny statement is specific.
questions.option_b: It is denied by the implicit deny rule.
questions.option_c: It is forwarded without being evaluated.
questions.option_d: It is permitted only if it uses UDP.
questions.explanation: Without an explicit permit statement, all traffic that does not match the Telnet deny rule is also dropped by the implicit deny.

questions.question: A company needs to prevent devices on 192.168.77.0/24 from initiating new TCP connections to 10.1.1.100 while allowing replies to connections initiated by the server. Which keyword is required by the lecture's ACL approach?
questions.option_a: host
questions.option_b: range
questions.option_c: established
questions.option_d: any
questions.explanation: The established keyword matches TCP packets with ACK or RST set, allowing qualifying return packets while excluding fresh SYN packets without ACK.

questions.question: A company uses a Standard ACL to block a particular source subnet. The administrator places the ACL near the source network. What is the main risk?
questions.option_a: The ACL may block traffic from that source to destinations that were never intended to be restricted.
questions.option_b: The ACL will automatically allow traffic to all public servers.
questions.option_c: The ACL will inspect destination ports and accidentally permit Telnet.
questions.option_d: The ACL will become an Extended ACL because of its placement.
questions.explanation: A Standard ACL cannot distinguish destinations. Applying it near the source can affect traffic to multiple destinations unnecessarily.

questions.question: A company wants external users to access a public web server in its DMZ, but the DMZ server must not initiate unrestricted connections to internal systems. Which policy design best follows the lecture?
questions.option_a: Permit all traffic between OUTSIDE, DMZ, and INSIDE.
questions.option_b: Allow OUTSIDE-to-INSIDE traffic but deny all OUTSIDE-to-DMZ traffic.
questions.option_c: Allow DMZ-to-INSIDE traffic without restrictions and block INSIDE-to-DMZ traffic.
questions.option_d: Permit specific OUTSIDE-to-DMZ services and deny or extremely restrict DMZ-to-INSIDE traffic.
questions.explanation: The three-zone design allows required public services to reach the DMZ while restricting movement from the exposed DMZ into the trusted internal network.

questions.question: A company uses a Zone-Based Firewall with INSIDE and OUTSIDE zones. It permits INSIDE-to-OUTSIDE communication. An administrator assumes this automatically permits OUTSIDE-to-INSIDE communication. What is wrong with this assumption?
questions.option_a: Zone policies are always bidirectional when one direction is permitted.
questions.option_b: Zone-pair policies are directional, and the reverse direction requires its own explicit policy.
questions.option_c: OUTSIDE-to-INSIDE traffic is controlled only by Standard ACLs.
questions.option_d: The INSIDE and OUTSIDE zones must be merged before communication is possible.
questions.explanation: ZBF zone-pair policies are directional and do not have to be symmetric. Permitting one direction does not automatically create an equivalent reverse-direction policy.

questions.question: A financial institution has sufficient budget and requires strong defence in depth for a public-facing DMZ. Which architecture is the strongest recommendation among the four designs covered in the lecture?
questions.option_a: Single firewall behind the border router.
questions.option_b: Single firewall in front of the border router.
questions.option_c: Dual firewall with the router before both firewalls.
questions.option_d: Single firewall positioned directly inside the DMZ.
questions.explanation: The dual-firewall screened-subnet design provides two separate security boundaries and genuine DMZ isolation, making it appropriate when defence in depth is the priority.

questions.question: A small business has a limited security budget and only one IT administrator. It wants a simple architecture with centralised firewall policy management. Which architecture is the most appropriate?
questions.option_a: Single firewall behind the border router.
questions.option_b: Dual firewall with the router before both firewalls.
questions.option_c: Dual firewall with the router between both firewalls.
questions.option_d: A design using three separate firewall devices.
questions.explanation: A single firewall behind the border router offers lower cost, simpler management, and one central point for policy management, although it introduces a single point of failure.

questions.question: An organisation chooses the dual-firewall architecture with the router positioned between both firewalls. Firewall 1 is successfully bypassed. Which component is directly exposed before traffic reaches the second firewall?
questions.option_a: The internal database server.
questions.option_b: The router.
questions.option_c: The internal employee workstation.
questions.option_d: The second firewall's management interface.
questions.explanation: In this architecture, the router sits between Firewall 1 and Firewall 2. If Firewall 1 is bypassed, the router is exposed before the second firewall.

questions.question: An administrator configures an ACL in the following order: 10 deny tcp any host 192.168.1.10 eq 23; 20 permit ip any any. A Telnet packet matches the first statement. What happens?
questions.option_a: The packet is permitted because the second statement allows all IP traffic.
questions.option_b: The packet is evaluated against both statements before a decision is made.
questions.option_c: The packet is denied immediately, and the second statement is not evaluated.
questions.option_d: The packet is denied only if the destination server is in the DMZ.
questions.explanation: ACLs use first-match processing. Once the Telnet packet matches the first deny statement, processing stops.

questions.question: An administrator wants to deny traffic from 10.10.30.0/24 to TCP destination port 23 on host 172.16.5.10 while allowing every other type of traffic. Which configuration correctly implements the policy?
questions.option_a: access-list 10 deny 10.10.30.0 0.0.0.255 followed by access-list 10 permit any.
questions.option_b: access-list 101 permit tcp 10.10.30.0 0.0.0.255 host 172.16.5.10 eq 23 followed by access-list 101 deny ip any any.
questions.option_c: access-list 101 deny udp 10.10.30.0 0.0.0.255 host 172.16.5.10 eq 23 followed by access-list 101 permit ip any any.
questions.option_d: access-list 101 deny tcp 10.10.30.0 0.0.0.255 host 172.16.5.10 eq 23 followed by access-list 101 permit ip any any.
questions.explanation: The Extended ACL matches the correct source subnet, destination host, TCP protocol, and Telnet port. The explicit permit statement allows all remaining traffic.

questions.question: An administrator needs to permit only source addresses in 192.168.50.0/28 through an interface. Which Standard ACL configuration correctly represents this requirement?
questions.option_a: access-list 10 permit 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.15
questions.option_c: access-list 110 permit tcp 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.15 any
questions.explanation: A /28 subnet has a wildcard mask of 0.0.0.15. The permit statement allows that source subnet, while the implicit deny blocks other sources.

questions.question: A numbered Extended ACL contains: access-list 110 deny tcp 192.168.40.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.50 eq 21; access-list 110 permit ip any any. Which Named ACL correctly preserves its behaviour?
questions.option_a: ip access-list standard DENY_FTP_ADMIN; deny 192.168.40.0 0.0.0.255; permit any
questions.option_b: ip access-list extended DENY_FTP_ADMIN; 10 deny tcp 192.168.40.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.50 eq 21; 20 permit ip any any
questions.option_c: ip access-list extended DENY_FTP_ADMIN; 10 permit tcp 192.168.40.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.50 eq 21; 20 deny ip any any
questions.option_d: ip access-list standard DENY_FTP_ADMIN; 10 deny tcp 192.168.40.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.50 eq 21; 20 permit ip any any
questions.explanation: The Named ACL must be extended because it matches TCP, source and destination addresses, and port 21. Preserving the original deny and permit order preserves its behaviour.

questions.question: A network administrator writes the following Extended ACL: access-list 101 deny tcp 192.168.77.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.100 established. What is the main logical error if the objective is to block new connections while allowing established return traffic?
questions.option_a: The established keyword can only be used with UDP.
questions.option_b: The ACL uses an invalid wildcard mask for a /24 network.
questions.option_c: The ACL denies qualifying established TCP packets instead of denying new SYN packets.
questions.option_d: The destination host must be specified using the any keyword.
questions.explanation: The established keyword matches TCP packets with ACK or RST set. Using deny with established blocks qualifying return traffic rather than specifically blocking new connection attempts.

questions.question: A network administrator wants to prevent new TCP connections from 192.168.77.0/24 to 10.1.1.100 while allowing replies to connections initiated by the server. Which ACL best implements the lecture's intended policy?
questions.option_a: access-list 101 permit tcp 192.168.77.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.100 established; access-list 101 deny tcp 192.168.77.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.100
questions.option_b: access-list 101 deny tcp 192.168.77.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.100 established; access-list 101 permit ip any any
questions.option_c: access-list 101 permit ip any any; access-list 101 deny tcp 192.168.77.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.100
questions.option_d: access-list 101 deny udp 192.168.77.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.100; access-list 101 permit tcp any any established
questions.explanation: The first statement permits qualifying TCP packets with ACK or RST set. The second denies other matching TCP traffic, including fresh SYN packets without ACK. The order is essential.

questions.question: A router has an Extended ACL applied inbound on the gateway interface of subnet 192.168.10.0/24. The ACL blocks Telnet traffic from that subnet to a particular server. Why is this placement appropriate?
questions.option_a: Extended ACLs can only operate on inbound interfaces.
questions.option_b: The ACL can stop unwanted traffic close to its source before it travels further into the network.
questions.option_c: Inbound ACLs automatically filter packets based on destination MAC addresses.
questions.option_d: The destination server must be connected directly to the same gateway interface.
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs can identify the exact destination, protocol, and port. Applying one near the source prevents unwanted traffic from travelling further into the network.

questions.question: A router has the following ACL entries: 10 deny ip 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any; 20 permit tcp host 192.168.1.5 host 192.168.2.10 eq 80. What happens to an HTTP packet from 192.168.1.5 to 192.168.2.10?
questions.option_a: It is permitted because the second statement specifically allows HTTP traffic.
questions.option_b: It is evaluated against the second statement before the first statement.
questions.option_c: It is permitted only if the destination server is in the same zone.
questions.option_d: It is denied because it matches the first statement, and ACL processing stops.
questions.explanation: The first statement denies all IP traffic from 192.168.1.0/24. The more specific HTTP permit statement is never reached because first-match processing stops at entry 10.

questions.question: A company has three firewall zones: INSIDE, OUTSIDE, and DMZ. It wants internal employees to access Internet services and public users to access only the company's web server in the DMZ. Which policy arrangement best satisfies these requirements?
questions.option_a: Permit INSIDE-to-OUTSIDE traffic, permit only required OUTSIDE-to-DMZ services, and deny or tightly restrict OUTSIDE-to-INSIDE traffic.
questions.option_b: Permit all OUTSIDE-to-INSIDE traffic and deny INSIDE-to-OUTSIDE traffic.
questions.option_c: Permit all traffic between all three zones because the DMZ is already isolated.
questions.option_d: Permit DMZ-to-INSIDE traffic and deny all communication between INSIDE and OUTSIDE.
questions.explanation: This design provides required employee Internet access and public access to DMZ services while preserving the separation between the external and internal networks.

questions.question: A company uses a single firewall behind its border router. The firewall fails. Which architectural weakness is demonstrated by this failure?
questions.option_a: The router automatically becomes the second independent firewall.
questions.option_b: The DMZ becomes physically separated from the internal network.
questions.option_c: The only firewall represents a single point of failure for the network.
questions.option_d: The network gains stronger defence in depth because one device is unavailable.
questions.explanation: A single-firewall architecture depends on one security device. Its failure removes the network's primary firewall boundary.

questions.question: An organisation deploys two firewalls to separate its DMZ from the internal network. During an audit, the administrator discovers that the two devices have inconsistent policies. What risk does this create?
questions.option_a: The two firewalls automatically merge their configurations.
questions.option_b: The inconsistent policies may create unintended traffic paths or security gaps despite the intended defence in depth.
questions.option_c: The router automatically corrects the policies using NAT.
questions.option_d: The DMZ becomes a trusted internal zone by default.
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies policy inconsistency between two firewalls as a real risk. Separate devices must be carefully coordinated to preserve the intended security boundaries.

questions.question: An administrator configures a Named Extended ACL with the name BLOCK_TELNET_TO_SERVER. Which configuration statement correctly enters the configuration sub-mode for this ACL?
questions.option_a: access-list extended BLOCK_TELNET_TO_SERVER
questions.option_b: ip access-list standard BLOCK_TELNET_TO_SERVER
questions.option_c: access-list 101 BLOCK_TELNET_TO_SERVER
questions.option_d: ip access-list extended BLOCK_TELNET_TO_SERVER
questions.explanation: The correct command is ip access-list extended followed by the ACL name. This enters the configuration sub-mode for a Named Extended ACL.

questions.question: An administrator creates a Named Extended ACL with entries numbered 10 and 30. A new deny statement must be inserted between them without deleting the existing entries. Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: Delete the entire ACL and recreate it with the new statement.
questions.option_b: Convert the ACL into a Standard ACL and add the statement.
questions.option_c: Insert a new statement using a sequence number such as 20.
questions.option_d: Change the ACL name to the number 20.
questions.explanation: Named ACL sequence numbers allow individual entries to be inserted at specific positions without rebuilding the entire ACL.

questions.question: A security administrator needs to block TCP traffic from subnet 192.168.10.0/24 to server 192.168.20.5 on destination port 23. Which option correctly identifies all required matching parameters?
questions.option_a: Source subnet 192.168.10.0/24, destination host 192.168.20.5, protocol TCP, destination port 23, action deny.
questions.option_b: Source host 192.168.20.5, destination subnet 192.168.10.0/24, protocol UDP, destination port 23, action permit.
questions.option_c: Source subnet 192.168.10.0/24, destination host 192.168.20.5, protocol IP, source port 23, action permit.
questions.option_d: Source subnet 192.168.10.0/24, destination host 192.168.20.5, protocol ICMP, destination port 23, action deny.
questions.explanation: The requirement specifies the source network, destination server, TCP protocol, and Telnet destination port. All these parameters must be matched by an Extended ACL.

questions.question: An administrator wants to allow TCP traffic from 192.168.1.0/24 to destination ports 20 through 25 on server 192.168.2.10. Which ACL parameter correctly represents the destination port range?
questions.option_b: range 20 25
questions.option_c: neq 20 25
questions.option_d: gt 20 lt 25
questions.explanation: The range operator matches an inclusive range of port numbers. The correct syntax is range 20 25.

questions.question: An Extended ACL contains the statement: access-list 101 deny tcp any host 192.168.10.10 eq 80. An administrator expects this to block every type of web communication to the server. What is the limitation of this statement?
questions.option_a: It blocks only UDP traffic on port 80.
questions.option_b: It blocks all IP traffic regardless of protocol.
questions.option_c: It blocks only packets originating from the destination server.
questions.option_d: It matches TCP traffic to destination port 80 only, not other protocols or ports.
questions.explanation: The statement explicitly matches TCP and destination port 80. Other protocols and destination ports are not matched by this particular deny entry.

questions.question: A company configures a Standard ACL to permit source subnet 192.168.100.0/27. It then applies the ACL to an interface through which traffic travels to several different destination networks. What is the key limitation of this configuration?
questions.option_a: The ACL can permit traffic only when the destination uses TCP.
questions.option_b: The ACL automatically permits traffic to all networks outside the subnet.
questions.option_c: The ACL cannot distinguish between the intended destination and other destinations, so its source-based filtering may affect more traffic than intended.
questions.option_d: The ACL becomes an Extended ACL when applied to multiple destination networks.
questions.explanation: A Standard ACL matches only source addresses. It cannot selectively permit or deny traffic based on destination, which is why placement near the destination is recommended.

questions.question: A network administrator wants to deny all UDP traffic from 10.0.0.0/8 to host 172.16.1.5 while permitting all remaining IP traffic. Which configuration is correct?
questions.option_a: access-list 101 deny tcp 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 host 172.16.1.5; access-list 101 permit ip any any
questions.option_b: access-list 101 deny udp 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 host 172.16.1.5; access-list 101 permit ip any any
questions.option_c: access-list 10 deny 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255; access-list 10 permit any
questions.option_d: access-list 101 permit udp 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 host 172.16.1.5; access-list 101 deny ip any any
questions.explanation: The Extended ACL uses UDP, the correct /8 wildcard mask, and the destination host. The final permit statement allows all other IP traffic.

questions.question: A network administrator applies an ACL inbound on GigabitEthernet0/1. Which packets are evaluated by this ACL?
questions.option_a: Packets entering the router through GigabitEthernet0/1.
questions.option_b: Packets leaving the router through GigabitEthernet0/1.
questions.option_c: All packets entering and leaving every router interface.
questions.option_d: Only packets generated by the router itself.
questions.explanation: An inbound ACL evaluates packets as they enter the router through the interface to which the ACL is applied.

questions.question: A router has an ACL applied outbound on GigabitEthernet0/1. A packet arrives through GigabitEthernet0/0 and is routed toward GigabitEthernet0/1. At which point is the outbound ACL evaluated?
questions.option_a: Before the packet enters GigabitEthernet0/0.
questions.option_b: Immediately after the packet reaches the router, regardless of its route.
questions.option_c: Only after the packet reaches its final destination host.
questions.option_d: As the packet leaves the router through GigabitEthernet0/1.
questions.explanation: An outbound ACL evaluates packets as they leave the router through the interface where the ACL is applied.

questions.question: An organisation wants its public-facing web server in the DMZ to be reachable from the Internet, but the internal database must remain inaccessible directly from external networks. Which design principle is most important?
questions.option_a: Place both servers in the same publicly accessible network segment.
questions.option_b: Use separate zones and explicitly control traffic between OUTSIDE, DMZ, and INSIDE.
questions.option_c: Permit unrestricted traffic from OUTSIDE to INSIDE and rely on server passwords.
questions.option_d: Remove the firewall between the DMZ and internal network.
questions.explanation: Zone separation and tailored directional policies allow public services to be exposed without directly exposing internal resources.

questions.question: A company wants a firewall architecture that filters inbound Internet traffic before it reaches the border router and also has a second firewall protecting the internal network. Which of the four architectures provides this arrangement?
questions.option_a: Single firewall behind the border router.
questions.option_b: Single firewall in front of the border router.
questions.option_c: Dual firewall with the router positioned between the two firewalls.
questions.option_d: Dual firewall with the router before both firewalls.
questions.explanation: The dual-firewall router-between design places Firewall 1 before the router and Firewall 2 after it, providing the specified filtering arrangement.

questions.question: An administrator configures a Standard ACL numbered 10 with the statement access-list 10 permit host 192.168.1.5. Which other statement is functionally equivalent for matching that exact source address?
questions.option_a: access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.5 0.0.0.0
questions.option_c: access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
questions.option_d: access-list 10 permit any 192.168.1.5
questions.explanation: The host keyword represents an exact single-address match, equivalent to explicitly using the wildcard mask 0.0.0.0.

questions.question: A company uses the dual-firewall screened-subnet architecture. During a review, the security team argues that using two firewalls guarantees that the internal network cannot be compromised. Which assessment is most accurate?
questions.option_a: The claim is correct because two firewalls make all attacks impossible.
questions.option_b: The claim is correct only if both firewalls use identical configurations.
questions.option_c: The claim is incorrect because the architecture provides no security benefit over a single firewall.
questions.option_d: The architecture strengthens defence in depth, but does not eliminate all attack possibilities or configuration risks.
questions.explanation: Two firewalls provide separate security boundaries, but security still depends on correct policies and implementation. The lecture also highlights policy inconsistency as a potential weakness.

questions.question: An administrator needs to create a Named ACL that permits only TCP traffic from 192.168.10.0/24 to host 192.168.20.5 on port 443, while denying all other traffic. Which configuration correctly expresses this policy?
questions.option_a: ip access-list standard ALLOW_HTTPS; permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255; deny any
questions.option_b: ip access-list extended ALLOW_HTTPS; deny tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.20.5 eq 443; permit ip any any
questions.option_c: ip access-list extended ALLOW_HTTPS; permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.20.5 eq 443
questions.option_d: ip access-list extended ALLOW_HTTPS; permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.20.5 eq 443; deny ip any any
questions.explanation: The Extended Named ACL precisely permits the required TCP source, destination, and port combination. The explicit deny statement blocks all remaining traffic.

questions.question: A network administrator configures the following entries: 10 permit tcp any host 192.168.1.10 eq 80; 20 deny ip any any. A packet from 10.0.0.5 to 192.168.1.10 uses TCP destination port 443. What happens?
questions.option_a: The packet is permitted because TCP is allowed by the first statement.
questions.option_b: The packet is denied because it does not match the first statement and matches the second statement.
questions.option_c: The packet is permitted because it originates from a valid IP address.
questions.option_d: The packet is evaluated against the implicit deny instead of statement 20.
questions.explanation: The first statement permits only TCP traffic to destination port 80. Port 443 does not match, so the packet reaches statement 20 and is denied.

questions.question: An administrator wants to block all traffic from source subnet 192.168.10.0/24 to a particular server, regardless of protocol or destination port. Which ACL approach is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: Standard ACL matching only the source subnet, placed near the destination.
questions.option_b: Extended ACL matching TCP destination port 23 only.
questions.option_c: Named ACL using the established keyword without any address matching.
questions.option_d: Standard ACL applied at the Internet-facing interface without considering other destinations.
questions.explanation: A Standard ACL can match the source subnet without protocol or port restrictions. Placing it near the intended destination minimises unintended effects on traffic to other networks.
